General Strike Disrupts Services and Businesses Across Bermuda

HAMILTON, Bermuda, June 17—A widespread general strike brought economic activity in Bermuda to a near-standstill on Monday, with public transport halted, government offices shuttered, and major employers including Axalta Coating Systems Ltd reporting significant operational disruptions.

The strike, called by the Bermuda Trade Union Congress (BTUC) late Sunday, follows weeks of stalled negotiations over wages and working conditions. Thousands of workers from a range of sectors—including transportation, sanitation, public administration, and manufacturing—joined picket lines or stayed home, severely impacting both public services and private industry.

Axalta Coating Systems Ltd, which operates a major facility in Hamilton, confirmed in a statement that production had been “substantially curtailed” due to the walkout. “We are working to maintain essential operations with the staff available,” said Rachel Simmons, spokesperson for the company. “However, the majority of our workforce is participating in the strike, and we anticipate continued delays until a resolution is reached.”

Ferries and buses were not running, leaving commuters stranded and traffic in central Hamilton unusually light. Garbage collection was suspended, and several schools were closed for the day. The Bermuda Chamber of Commerce estimated that the strike could cost the island’s economy upwards of $1.5 million for each day of disruption, warning that extended action could have far-reaching consequences for tourism and international business.

The BTUC said the strike would continue until the government returned to the bargaining table with “meaningful proposals.” “Our members have sent a clear message today: enough is enough,” said BTUC president Andrew Trott at a midday rally outside the Cabinet Office, attended by an estimated 2,000 demonstrators. “We are prepared to stand strong for as long as it takes.”

Premier Lauren Haynes urged both sides to resume talks, expressing concern about the knock-on effects for Bermuda’s reputation as a business and tourism destination. “We respect the rights of workers to advocate for fair treatment, but we must also safeguard the functioning of our island community,” Haynes said in a televised address.

Local analysts noted that the strike’s broad participation marked the largest labor stoppage in Bermuda in over a decade. “This is a pivotal moment for labor relations here,” said economic analyst Peter Rawlins. “How quickly it is resolved will determine the impact not just for workers, but for the entire economy.”

As of Monday evening, negotiations had not resumed, and union leaders said the strike would continue into Tuesday.
